note: Prices are working estimates for the UK private-sale market, not quotes. Re-check against eBay sold listings before offering.

items.name: Panasonic Lumix S5 II / S5 IIX
items.spec: Full-frame 24MP, proper phase-detect autofocus at last, in-body stabilisation, 6K open gate, and no recording time limit. Dual native ISO handles dim interiors without the noise penalty.
items.flop: Panasonic has almost no mindshare against Sony and Canon in stills, and the L-mount puts buyers off because they assume the lens choice is thin. It is not, but the assumption prices the body.
items.catch: L-mount glass costs more used than E-mount. Body is chunky for a hybrid. Check shutter count and the rear screen hinge ribbon.
items.why: Business kit for interiors: open gate plus strong low light suits dim pub and venue work where you are fighting mixed lighting.

items.name: DJI Mavic 3 Classic
items.spec: Four-thirds Hasselblad sensor, 46 minutes of flight, 15km transmission. Sensor area is roughly four times a Mini's, which is the whole difference in dynamic range on a bright exterior.
items.flop: DJI launched it beside the Mavic 3 Pro's triple-camera setup and every review led with the Pro. The Classic is the same airframe and the same main sensor, with the two niche lenses removed.
items.catch: Check the C-class marking on the airframe label before you buy, it changes what you can legally do. Must be unbound from the seller's DJI account. Check battery cycle counts in the app, not the seller's word.
items.why: Business kit: a genuine sensor-size step up for commercial exteriors at under half the price of current kit.

items.name: Minisforum UM790 Pro / Beelink SER8
items.spec: Eight-core Ryzen 7840HS or 8845HS, takes 64GB of DDR5 and two NVMe drives, dual 2.5GbE, draws about 15W idle, fits in a litre of space.
items.flop: Neither brand has a high street presence or a marketing budget. Buyers comparing specs end up with a Dell or an Intel NUC at twice the price because those names feel safer.
items.catch: BIOS and firmware support is patchy and updates come from forum links, not an update tool. Fan noise varies unit to unit. Warranty claims mean shipping to a depot abroad.
items.why: Business kit, and the one on this list most likely to change your monthly numbers. One of these at home running Proxmox will host your n8n stack and double as a render and stitching box, replacing a VPS line item with a one-off.

items.name: Dell UltraSharp U2723QE / U3223QE
items.spec: 4K IPS Black panel at roughly 2000:1, so blacks hold up far better than normal IPS. Built-in KVM and a 90W USB-C hub, so one cable carries video, power and every peripheral.
items.flop: Monitors are sold on refresh rate and curve. A 60Hz productivity panel gets no shelf space and no YouTube coverage, so corporate units flood the market with nobody bidding.
items.catch: 60Hz only, so no good for gaming. Off-lease units can have backlight bleed or uniformity issues at the corners, which you cannot see in a photo. Insist on a photo of a full-black screen in a dark room.
items.why: Keep. Replaces a separate dock, which is a real saving most people forget to count.

items.name: Dell WD19TBS / HP Thunderbolt G5 dock
items.spec: Thunderbolt 3, dual 4K out, gigabit ethernet, five USB ports, and 130W or 180W of laptop charging over one cable.
items.flop: Accessories get zero marketing and are written off the books with the laptop. They end up in office clearance lots priced as e-waste while people buy £200 generic hubs that deliver 60W and drop displays.
items.catch: The dock is useless without the matching power brick, so never buy one listed without it. Firmware updates often need the vendor's own utility and a supported host machine.
items.why: Flip. Enough steady demand from home-office buyers that these do move, and the margin on a £40 buy is strong.

items.name: Fujifilm X-H2
items.spec: 40MP APS-C sensor, 8K video, in-body stabilisation, weather-sealed pro body with a top LCD and a proper grip. The resolution is genuinely useful for architectural and interior detail.
items.flop: Fujifilm launched the retro-styled X-T5 within weeks, with the same sensor. Every reviewer and every enthusiast went for the dials and the looks, and the better-built body got ignored.
items.catch: 40MP is unforgiving of soft glass, so budget for decent lenses. Wants CFexpress Type B cards for the fast modes, which are not cheap. Battery drains faster than the X-T5.
items.why: Keep. Resolution plus weather sealing is a working combination for site stills.

items.name: Insta360 ONE RS 1-Inch 360 Edition
items.spec: Twin one-inch Leica-co-engineered sensors shooting 6K 360. Still the largest sensors in a consumer 360 camera, which shows immediately in low light and in highlight roll-off through windows.
items.flop: Insta360's marketing pushed the X3 and everything after it, all of which use far smaller sensors but look sleeker and sell on viral social clips. The better-imaging model was quietly left behind.
items.catch: Not waterproof without the case. The exposed lenses scratch easily and guards are a separate purchase, so budget for them. Stitching workflow is slower than current models.
items.why: Business kit: fast scouting and rough-cut walkthroughs ahead of a proper bracketed DSLR shoot, without dragging the tripod round twice.

items.name: ASUS ProArt Studiobook / ProArt P16
items.spec: Calibrated OLED panel out of the box, discrete RTX graphics, full-size SD Express slot, and a physical control dial that maps to Adobe and video tools.
items.flop: ASUS spends its marketing on ROG gaming machines, and creative buyers default to a MacBook Pro without shopping around. ProArt sits in the middle with nobody advertising to it.
items.catch: Heavy, and the fans are audible under load. OLED panels on used units can carry burn-in from taskbars, so ask for a photo of a full-white screen. Resale is slow.
items.why: Keep. Colour-accurate panel plus a GPU is the combination you otherwise pay Apple a premium for.

items.name: Dell Precision 5570 / ThinkPad P1 Gen 5
items.spec: XPS-grade chassis with workstation graphics, 4K panel options, and support for 64GB of RAM and two NVMe drives. Certified drivers for CAD and 3D work.
items.flop: Corporate fleets dump these on three-year cycles. Private buyers do not know that "Precision" means an XPS with a professional GPU in it, so they scroll past and buy a consumer laptop for more money.
items.catch: Thermal throttling is real under sustained load, so check the fans spin freely. Batteries at this age are often at 60% health. Watch for BIOS supervisor passwords and active asset-management locks.
items.why: Flip, with a caveat: these move well to anyone doing 3D or CAD, and a RAM and SSD top-up from your donor stock lifts the sale price more than it costs.

items.name: Technics EAH-A800
items.spec: Around 50 hours of battery with noise cancelling on, LDAC support, and a genuinely good eight-microphone call setup that beats most of the big names on voice clarity.
items.flop: Technics is a Panasonic hi-fi brand nobody associates with headphones. It gets no shelf space next to Sony and Bose, so it competes on nothing but spec sheets that buyers never read.
items.catch: Build feels plastic for the price. The app is basic next to Sony's. Check the headband padding and the folding hinges, which are the usual failure points.
items.why: Flip. Low enough buy-in that even slow movement leaves margin, and counterfeits are not a problem because nobody bothers faking it.

items.name: Sennheiser Momentum 4 Wireless
items.spec: Around 60 hours of playback, which is roughly double the Sony equivalent, with the best plain sound quality in the price bracket and a proper parametric EQ in the app.
items.flop: Sennheiser's consumer arm changed hands and the marketing spend evaporated. The design is also deliberately plain, which kills it on a shop shelf against Sony and Bose.
items.catch: Noise cancelling is a step behind the Sony XM5. No folding hinge, so the case is bulky. Early units had a firmware fault that drained the battery in standby, so confirm it has been updated.
items.why: Flip. The audio crowd knows these, so there is a real buyer pool even if the general public does not.

items.name: LG gram 16 / 17
items.spec: A 17-inch screen at around 1.35kg, with an 80Wh battery. Nothing else puts that much screen in that little weight, and it still runs a full day unplugged.
items.flop: LG is a TV and appliance brand in most buyers' heads. It has no laptop presence in UK retail, so the gram sells almost entirely to people who already went looking for it.
items.catch: The chassis flexes, which is the price of the weight. Speakers are poor. Integrated graphics only, so no good for rendering. Check the hinges and the lid for stress cracks.
items.why: Keep. If you are carrying a machine round sites all day, the weight difference is the feature.

items.name: HONOR Magic7 Pro
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 5270mAh, and a 200MP periscope that is one of the better long-range phone cameras made. Sold officially in the UK, so it carries a real warranty and proper network support.
items.flop: Honor has had no brand equity in the UK since the Huawei split. It sells a flagship the equal of a Galaxy S25 and the public reads the badge as a budget brand, so it depreciates like one.
items.catch: Update commitment is shorter than Samsung's or Google's, so check what it is still receiving. MagicOS is heavy on duplicate apps. Check the curved screen edges for pressure marks.
items.why: Keep, and the best risk-adjusted phone on this list: UK stock, UK warranty, grey-import pricing without the grey-import problems.

items.name: Xiaomi 15 Ultra
items.spec: One-inch main sensor with Leica tuning, a 200MP periscope, Snapdragon 8 Elite and 5410mAh. In pure camera hardware terms it outguns anything Apple or Samsung shipped that year.
items.flop: Xiaomi sells officially in the UK but spends almost nothing on brand advertising here, and most buyers still file it under cheap. A £1,299 Xiaomi was always going to sit on shelves.
items.catch: The camera is only as good as the processing, and Xiaomi's has been inconsistent across updates. HyperOS ships with bloat. Confirm it is the global ROM and not a converted Chinese unit.
items.why: Keep. If you want a pocket camera that genuinely holds up for stills, this is the most camera per pound in the list.

items.name: Vivo X200 Pro / OPPO Find X8 Pro
items.spec: Dimensity 9400, 6000mAh and 5910mAh respectively, Zeiss and Hasselblad camera systems with genuinely excellent periscope telephotos. Both are top-tier hardware by any measure.
items.flop: Neither brand sells properly in the UK. With no retail presence, no carrier deals and no advertising, the only buyers are people who already knew what they wanted.
items.catch: This is the risky one. Grey import means no UK warranty and no local repair route. VoLTE and WiFi calling are frequently broken on UK networks, which means no calls on 4G or 5G. Confirm it is a global ROM with Play Services, not a Chinese ROM, and confirm VoLTE works on your network before money changes hands.
items.why: Keep, if and only if you verify VoLTE on your own SIM first. Fail that check and it is an expensive iPod.

items.name: Sony Xperia 1 VII
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 5000mAh, headphone jack, microSD, and the manual camera controls Sony keeps shipping while everyone else removes them. 4K OLED display.
items.flop: Same story as every Xperia: no UK carrier presence, no advertising, a price nobody would pay for a brand with no heat behind it. Sony sells these to people who hunt them down.
items.catch: Early units had a faulty circuit board causing random shutdowns, and Sony ran a replacement programme from July 2025. Dial *#06# for the IMEI and run it through Sony's own IMEI checker before you buy. If the seller will not give you the IMEI, walk.
items.why: Keep. Verify the IMEI first, then it is one of the best value flagships going.

items.name: OnePlus 13
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 6000mAh silicon-carbon battery, 100W wired charging, and a properly good display. Battery life was among the best in its year.
items.flop: OnePlus lost its enthusiast identity when it merged software with OPPO, and never built a mainstream one to replace it. It now sits in a gap: too expensive for bargain hunters, too obscure for flagship buyers.
items.catch: Silicon-carbon batteries are newer chemistry with less of a track record, and replacements are hard to source in the UK. Check charging behaviour at high percentages. No official UK carrier support.
items.why: Flip. The enthusiast pool still knows and wants OnePlus, so these actually move, unlike most of this list.

items.name: Galaxy S25 Edge
items.spec: Snapdragon 8 Elite, 6.7in display, and an unusually thin body. On paper the discount looks like every other entry on this page.
items.flop: It did not flop for want of marketing. Samsung promoted it hard. It flopped because a 3900mAh battery in a 6.7in flagship means it runs out before the day does, and thinness turned out to be a feature nobody had asked for.
items.catch: The discount is the market pricing a real defect, not an oversight. Thin bodies also mean less room for heat, so sustained performance drops off. Resale will keep sliding.
items.why: Trap, and it is on this list as the control case. Before buying any steep discount, ask whether the thing was ignored or rejected. Ignored is a sleeper. Rejected is just a cheap bad product.

items.name: Lenovo ThinkCentre M720q / M920q Tiny
items.spec: A one-litre desktop with a proper quad or six-core desktop chip, two RAM slots, an NVMe slot and a 2.5in bay. Draws about 10W idle and is effectively silent.
items.flop: Office clearance stock with no consumer marketing behind it. People shopping for a small PC see a Raspberry Pi or a new NUC and never learn that a far more capable machine sells for the price of the Pi's case and PSU.
items.catch: Often sold with no power brick, which is a proprietary square tip, so check. Some are locked with a BIOS supervisor password. The 35W T-series chips are slower than the 65W ones for the same money, so read the exact model number.
items.why: Business kit at pocket-money prices. Two of these will run your n8n stack and a backup target with change from £200. Cheapest route off a VPS bill there is.

items.name: Sennheiser HD 560S / HD 599
items.spec: Genuinely neutral reference tuning, replaceable pads and cable, comfortable for hours. If you are cutting audio for client videos, these tell you what is actually in the file.
items.flop: Wired headphones with no noise cancelling and no brand heat. They are sold to a audio crowd that already knows about them and advertised to nobody else.
items.catch: Open-back, so everyone near you hears them and they leak in noise. No use on a train or a shoot. Check the headband for the known crack point where the slider meets the cup.
items.why: Keep. Buy for the editing desk, not for travel.

items.name: Reolink PoE cameras + NVR
items.spec: 4K or 5MP over a single ethernet run, records locally to the NVR or a NAS, works over RTSP with anything. No subscription, no cloud account required.
items.flop: Ring and Nest spend fortunes on advertising a monthly fee. Reolink sells hardware that needs no fee, which means no recurring revenue to fund advertising, which means nobody has heard of it.
items.catch: Running cable is the real cost, not the camera. The phone app is functional rather than polished. Check the firmware is current and the unit is not an older model that phones home to a region you do not want.
items.why: Keep. Covers your own premises and kit storage for a one-off cost instead of a direct debit.

items.name: TP-Link Omada EAP access points
items.spec: Ceiling or wall APs with PoE, proper VLAN and guest network support, and a free controller you can run on any machine, including one of those Tiny PCs.
items.flop: Ubiquiti owns the entire conversation about prosumer networking through sheer community presence. Omada does the same job for roughly half the money and has almost no mindshare outside installers.
items.catch: You need PoE, so budget for a PoE switch or injectors. Controller versions and hardware revisions have to match, so check the revision number on the label, not the listing title.
items.why: Flip, with decent margin. Small businesses and installers buy these, and the buyer pool knows what it is looking at.

items.name: Brother mono laser (HL-L2350DW class)
items.spec: Duplex mono laser, wireless, and toner that costs pence per page from third parties. Sits unused for months and still prints first time, which inkjets famously do not.
items.flop: HP and Epson spend their marketing on ink subscription models, because that is where the money is. A printer that costs almost nothing to run after purchase has nobody advertising it.
items.catch: Check the page count in the menu before buying and confirm the drum unit life remaining, which is separate from toner. Avoid units where a starter toner is the only one included.
items.why: Keep. Boring, and it will quietly save you more per year than most things on this list.

items.name: Zoom H1essential / Tascam DR-05X
items.spec: 32-bit float recording on the newer Zooms, which means a clipped take is recoverable in the edit. Runs off AA batteries, records to microSD, takes a lav via 3.5mm.
items.flop: Audio recorders are bought by a small professional crowd and advertised to nobody. Everyone else assumes the camera microphone will do, finds out it will not, and still never goes looking for one of these.
items.catch: Built-in mics are fine for room tone and poor for interviews, so budget for a lav. Check the 3.5mm jack for crackle by wiggling a plug in it. Older DR-05 models are not 32-bit float, which is the whole point.
items.why: Business kit. If you ever record a client talking about their venue for a walkthrough or a social clip, clean audio is what makes it look professional.

items.name: Panasonic Lumix G9 / GX9 (Micro Four Thirds)
items.spec: Weather-sealed body, excellent in-body stabilisation, and a high-resolution mode that composites a 80MP file from sensor shifts. Lenses are small, sharp and cheap because the whole system collapsed in price.
items.flop: The industry narrative decided full-frame had won and Micro Four Thirds was finished. Bodies and glass fell through the floor on sentiment rather than on performance.
items.catch: Smaller sensor, so low light is a real step behind full-frame. The format's future is genuinely uncertain, which caps resale. Check the shutter count and the rubber grips, which go sticky with age.
items.why: Keep. The stabilisation and the cheap sharp glass make it a strong second body for handheld interior work.

items.name: DJI Mic 2 / Mic Mini
items.spec: Two transmitters and a receiver in a charging case, 32-bit float internal recording on the Mic 2, and onboard backup recording so a dropout does not kill the take.
items.flop: This is not a marketing failure, it is an abandonment one. Bought for a YouTube channel that lasted four videos. Comes back to market boxed, barely used, with every clip and cable still bagged.
items.catch: Check all three units charge and pair, not just the receiver. The magnetic clips get lost first, so confirm they are present. Verify the case hinge and that the lid closes flush.
items.why: Flip. Creators are a steady buyer pool and these move reliably. The condition on abandoned kit means you can list it as near-new.

items.name: Elgato Stream Deck / Key Light / capture cards
items.spec: The Stream Deck is a programmable macro pad that runs anything you can script, not just streaming. Key Lights are properly colour-accurate panels controllable from the desktop.
items.flop: Pandemic-era streaming ambitions that did not survive contact with reality. Enormous volume of this stuff came to market when people went back to the office and stopped streaming.
items.catch: Capture cards date fast, so check the model supports the resolution you want. Stream Deck software is account-tied but the hardware is not locked. Key Light power bricks go missing.
items.why: Keep the Stream Deck. Mapped to your editing and stitching shortcuts it is a genuine time saver, and nothing else does that job for £50.

items.name: DJI Osmo Mobile 5 / 6 gimbal
items.spec: Three-axis phone stabiliser, folds flat, built-in extension rod on the later models. Turns a walked shot through a venue from unusable to smooth.
items.flop: Classic drawer gear. Bought for one holiday, used once, folded away. Volume on the used market is enormous and prices reflect it.
items.catch: Test all three motors hold under load with a phone fitted, not empty. The clamp arms crack. Check the folding joint is not loose. Missing counterweights and tripod feet are common.
items.why: Flip, cheaply and often. Low buy-in, steady demand, and they ship easily.

items.name: Huion Kamvas / XP-Pen Artist pen displays
items.spec: Screen you draw directly on, 8192 pressure levels, battery-free pen. The panels on the newer ones are laminated and colour-calibrated, which was a Wacom-only feature at four times the money.
items.flop: Two causes stacked: Wacom owns the brand conversation entirely, and these are a textbook new-hobby purchase that gets abandoned when the drawing habit does not stick.
items.catch: Pen nibs wear out and spares get lost, so check some are included. Test for parallax and dead pixels. The three-cable setup is fiddly and the breakout cable is proprietary, so it must be present.
items.why: Keep if you do any retouching or masking work. Far faster than a mouse for cutting people out of pano stitches.

items.name: Entry 3D printers (Ender 3 / Prusa Mini class)
items.spec: Usually sold with hundreds of pounds of upgrades already fitted by an owner who went deep for three months: better hotend, auto-levelling, upgraded board, spare nozzles, part-used filament.
items.flop: Highest abandonment rate of anything in consumer tech. The gap between buying a printer and reliably printing something useful defeats most people inside a season.
items.catch: Check the bed is not warped by looking down its length. Ask for a photo of a recent print, not a photo of the machine. Seized Z-rods and stripped extruder gears are the usual faults. Collection only, realistically.
items.why: Flip. The upgrades are free money because sellers almost never price them in, and the buyer pool knows exactly what those parts are worth.

items.name: Lenovo Legion Go
items.spec: An 8.8-inch 144Hz 1600p screen, Z1 Extreme chip, and detachable controllers. The biggest and sharpest display in the handheld class by a clear margin.
items.flop: It arrived beside the Steam Deck OLED, and Valve owned the conversation entirely. Windows handhelds also carry a reputation for software jank that put off the mainstream buyer.
items.catch: Battery life is poor at high settings. Windows handheld software is genuinely fiddly. Test both detachable controllers for stick drift and check the hall-effect sticks are the later revision.
items.why: Flip. Gaming handhelds still turn over faster than anything else on this list.

items.name: HP t630 / t640 thin clients (and Dell Wyse)
items.spec: Fanless, palm-sized, VESA-mountable, and designed to run 24/7 bolted to a wall. The AMD-based t630 and t640 handle 1080p video and a full browser without complaint, and draw about 7W.
items.flop: Sold only to IT departments buying a thousand at a time and never advertised to a single human being. When the lease ends they go out by the pallet, and nobody bidding knows what they are.
items.catch: The weaker Intel-based models choke on video, so hold out for the AMD t630 or t640. Many ship with 8GB of flash storage and want an mSATA or M.2 drive adding. Confirm the power brick is included.
items.why: Business kit, and the cheapest way to put a screen on a wall. Fanless matters in a quiet bar, where a whirring box behind the telly gets noticed.

items.name: Ex-corporate 24in IPS (Dell P-series / HP EliteDisplay)
items.spec: 24in 1080p or 1440p IPS, height adjustable, pivots to portrait, and built for a three-year on-site warranty. Frequently sold in matched pairs from the same office.
items.flop: Monitors are advertised on refresh rate, curve and gaming badges. A matte 60Hz office panel gets no coverage anywhere, so clearance stock lands in a market with nobody bidding.
items.catch: Often listed without the stand or cables, and a replacement stand costs more than the monitor. Ask for photos of a full-white and a full-black screen to catch uniformity problems and taskbar burn-in.
items.why: Flip, in pairs. This is the workhorse tier below the UltraSharp entry on this list: home-office buyers want two matching screens, and a pair at £70 moves faster than two singles.

items.name: Dell Latitude 7490 / HP EliteBook 830
items.spec: 14in business chassis, 8th gen Intel or newer, takes 32GB of RAM and an NVMe drive, spill-resistant keyboard, and a battery you can actually replace. Built to survive five years of daily abuse.
items.flop: Latitude and EliteBook mean nothing to a consumer. Someone shopping at this price buys a new plastic Celeron from a supermarket instead, because it has a brand they recognise and comes in a box.
items.catch: Check for BIOS supervisor passwords and active asset-management locks, which make a machine worthless for resale. Batteries at this age are often at 60% health. Get the exact chip model, not just 'i5'.
items.why: Flip, and probably the best margin per hour here. A £100 buy plus RAM and an SSD from your donor stock sells at £220 to £260 without much effort.

items.name: ScanSnap iX500 / iX1500 document scanner
items.spec: Duplex sheet-fed scanner that pulls 25 double-sided pages a minute straight into searchable PDF. Still faster and more dependable than most things you can buy new at twice the price.
items.flop: Discontinued, and the brand moved from Fujitsu to Ricoh, which lost the few buyers who were paying attention. Scanners get no marketing at all, because everyone assumes a phone camera will do the job.
items.catch: The rubber pick rollers wear out every few thousand sheets and are a £20 part. Older units want the legacy ScanSnap Manager software rather than the current app, so ask the seller which they used.
items.why: Keep. If you ever digitise receipts, contracts or site paperwork, this clears a shoebox in an afternoon rather than a weekend.

items.name: Focusrite Scarlett 2i2 (1st / 2nd gen)
items.spec: Two XLR inputs with phantom power, clean preamps, and latency low enough for voice work. For anything short of a professional studio it does the same job as the current generation.
items.flop: Focusrite markets each new generation hard, which makes the previous one read as obsolete overnight even though nothing meaningful changed. Huge numbers of them exist.
items.catch: 1st gen driver support on current Windows is patchy, so prefer 2nd gen. Turn the gain knobs with something plugged in to check for crackle. The USB-B cable is usually missing.
items.why: Flip. Anyone starting a podcast or recording voiceover needs one, and that buyer pool never dries up.

items.name: DJI Osmo Pocket 2
items.spec: A three-axis mechanical gimbal in something the size of a highlighter pen. The footage is locked-down smooth in a way no phone's software stabilisation matches, and the four-mic array records usable audio.
items.flop: Buried by the launch noise around the Pocket 3 and its larger sensor. The Pocket 2 still does the one thing it was bought for, and most were bought for a single holiday.
items.catch: Small sensor, so low light is weak. Accessories are proprietary and the wide-angle adapter is almost always missing. Power it on and check the gimbal holds level and does not buzz at rest.
items.why: Business kit. Walking a venue grabbing smooth clips for social is exactly its job, and it rides in a jacket pocket alongside the pano kit.

items.name: Panasonic GX80 / Olympus E-M10 (entry MFT)
items.spec: Pocketable rangefinder-style body with in-body stabilisation and 4K, taking the same cheap sharp Micro Four Thirds glass as the bigger bodies. A 20mm f/1.7 pancake runs about £120 used.
items.flop: The same sentiment collapse that took the G9 down, but harder at this end, because entry-level bodies are the first thing people dump once a format gets declared dead.
items.catch: No weather sealing and no real grip. Older sensors get noisy above ISO 1600. Check the shutter count, and test the viewfinder for dead lines, which is the common fault.
items.why: Keep, as the cheap way into the system. If the G9 entry appeals but not at £300, this is the same glass on a smaller body.

items.name: Manfrotto 055 / 190 aluminium tripods
items.spec: Aluminium legs rated far beyond what a mirrorless body weighs, still repairable with parts you can buy. The horizontal centre-column models put a camera directly over a table or out down a stairwell.
items.flop: Every tripod advert for a decade has sold carbon fibre and travel weight. Heavy aluminium legs that outlive their owner get no coverage, so they sit on Marketplace at scrap prices.
items.catch: Heavy, which is the entire reason they are cheap. Check the leg locks hold under load and the centre column does not slip. Heads are often sold separately, so confirm exactly what is included.
items.why: Keep. For panorama work a solid tripod beats a light one, because every bit of shift between frames turns into a stitching error later.

items.name: Panoramic heads (Nodal Ninja, Manfrotto 303)
items.spec: Rails and rotators that sit the lens's no-parallax point over the axis of rotation, with click stops at set intervals. That is the whole difference between frames that stitch cleanly and frames that fight you.
items.flop: A tiny buyer pool, shrinking further as people assume a one-shot 360 camera has replaced the job. Nobody advertises these, and sellers leaving the hobby just want the space back.
items.catch: Compatibility matters, because the rail has to suit your body and lens. Missing click-stop rings and Allen keys are common, and they are fiddly to source. Measure before committing.
items.why: Business kit, and the most directly useful thing on this list for you. A spare rig in the car means a failed head on site costs you an hour, not the shoot.

items.name: Meta Quest 2
items.spec: Standalone headset with full positional tracking, needing no PC and no base stations. Its browser will open a 360 panorama or a web-published walkthrough directly.
items.flop: The purest drawer gear on this list. Bought at Christmas, worn for a fortnight of novelty, then left in a cupboard, because almost nobody keeps putting a headset on.
items.catch: Battery health degrades badly in units left flat for years. The foam facial interface is unhygienic secondhand, so budget £15 to replace it. Meta's software support for this model will not run forever.
items.why: Keep, as a sales prop rather than a gadget. Handing a publican or a principal a headset showing their own building is a different conversation from showing them a laptop.

items.name: Brother P-touch / Dymo LabelWriter
items.spec: Thermal printers that need no ink at all. The desktop LabelWriter models fire address and barcode labels off a PC at speed; the handheld P-touch units do cable and shelf labels anywhere.
items.flop: Textbook razor and blades. The manufacturer makes its money on tape, so the printers are near-given away and advertised to nobody.
items.catch: Consumables are the real cost, and genuine Brother TZe tape is not cheap. Third-party tape works but quality varies. Run a test label before paying, and skip any unit with a cracked cassette door.
items.why: Keep. Labelled cables and boxes on an install is a small thing that makes the difference between looking like a company and looking like a bloke with a van.

items.name: APC Back-UPS / Smart-UPS
items.spec: Battery backup that rides out the brownouts and half-second cuts that corrupt a running machine, plus surge protection. Smart-UPS models report over USB so a machine can shut itself down cleanly.
items.flop: Sold to IT buyers and invisible to everyone else. Most of the ones on the used market are listed as faulty when the only fault is a battery that has reached the end of its life.
items.catch: Assume the battery is dead. Replacement sealed lead-acid cells run £20 to £35 and swap out in about ten minutes. They are heavy, so postage ruins the deal: buy local or not at all.
items.why: Business kit. A signage box that corrupts its drive during a power blink is a drive to Newtownabbey you did not need to make.

items.name: 8-port PoE switches (TP-Link / Netgear)
items.spec: Eight ports with power delivered over four or eight of them, so cameras and access points run off a single cable with no socket needed at the far end.
items.flop: Nobody advertises network switches to the public. They come out of office clearance beside the docks and monitors, priced as scrap by sellers who have no idea what PoE is worth.
items.catch: Read the total power budget on the label rather than counting ports, because a 55W switch will not carry four hungry cameras. Fanned models whine, so prefer fanless anywhere people sit.
items.why: Flip, and it pairs with the Reolink and Omada entries. If you are buying those for a job, pick the switch up in the same week.

items.name: Synology DS220+ / DS720+
items.spec: Two bays, dual gigabit, and DSM, which is still the best NAS software anyone ships. Synology Drive gives you the thing you are actually trying to replace: file sync across machines, running on hardware you own.
items.flop: Barely flops at all, and that is the point. Synology holds value better than almost any consumer hardware, so the discount is thin and the bargains are specific rather than general.
items.catch: Because the unit price is firm, the deal is always in the drives. A DS220+ listed with two populated 4TB disks for £205 is the bargain, not a bare unit at £240. Check drive power-on hours in DSM before buying, and treat any disk past 40,000 hours as a spare.
items.why: Business kit, and the answer to the Google Drive problem. Sync between the desktop and the MacBook without Drive in the middle, which is what was creating three versions of everything.

items.name: Rode Wireless GO (1st gen)
items.spec: Clip-on transmitter with a mic built in, and a receiver that mounts on a camera or feeds a phone. No cables, no boom, and it holds up across a room.
items.flop: Two causes stacked: superseded by the GO II, which took all the marketing, and bought in volume by people who filmed four videos and stopped.
items.catch: 1st gen has no onboard backup recording, so a dropout is lost audio for good. The output cable is easily lost and awkward to replace. Pair both units and test at ten metres before paying.
items.why: Flip. Sits below the DJI Mic entry on price with the same buyer pool, so it moves to the creators who cannot stretch to the DJI.

items.name: Garmin Epix Gen 2
items.spec: AMOLED screen, full onboard maps, multi-band GPS and the whole Firstbeat training stack. Inside it is very close to the Fenix 7 Pro AMOLED, and it keeps getting features handed down from the Pro range.
items.flop: The Epix Pro arrived a year later and took the name recognition. The market now confuses the two, overpays for the Pro, and leaves the Gen 2 sitting at a fraction of its £799 launch price.
items.catch: Battery is shorter than a Fenix 7, and always-on display drains it hard. No solar. Gen 2 (42/47mm) and Gen 2 Pro (bigger case, torch, better heart-rate sensor) get listed under the same name, so check which one it is before paying Pro money.
items.why: The one to have if you want a proper smartwatch screen without giving up Garmin battery life and maps.

items.name: Garmin Fenix 7 Pro Solar / Sapphire Solar
items.spec: Multi-band GPS, full maps, solar charging, built-in torch and the newer Elevate v4 heart-rate sensor. Battery runs into weeks rather than days.
items.flop: Fenix 8 landed in 2024 and pulled used Fenix 7 prices down by about 40%. Nothing about the 7 Pro got worse. It just stopped being the newest one.
items.catch: The MIP screen looks dull next to AMOLED, and the watch is big and heavy. The bezel picks up dings. There are a lot of variants (7S / 7 / 7X × Solar / Sapphire / Pro), so match the listing to the exact model.
items.why: Best all-round outdoor watch per pound right now. Expensive at launch, mid-range money used.

items.name: Garmin Instinct 2X Solar
items.spec: Rugged case, solar charging, multi-week battery, a full-size GPS antenna, and a built-in torch, which is rare at this price.
items.flop: It sits under the base Instinct 2 in search results, and buyers assume they are the same watch. They are not. The 2X is the one with the torch and the bigger battery.
items.catch: No maps. The buttons are easy to press by accident and the screen is small. A base Instinct 2 is fairly priced, so don't pay 2X money for one.
items.why: Watch that lives on site, in the van or on the hill and never needs charging on a weekly trip.

items.name: Garmin Forerunner 255 Music
items.spec: Same training stack as the 265, multi-band GPS, about a week of battery from the MIP screen, and onboard music storage with offline Spotify on the Music version.
items.flop: The Forerunner 265 is basically an AMOLED 255, and it got all the attention. That leaves the 255 underpriced, and the Music version often sells for about the same as the base model.
items.catch: Check it really is the Music version (255 Music / 255S Music). That is worth £25–£40 by itself. The MIP screen looks dated next to the 265.
items.why: Runners know the model names, so it sells fast. Easy to buy right and move on.

items.name: Garmin Venu 2 Plus
items.spec: AMOLED screen, speaker and mic so you can take calls through your phone, voice assistant, Elevate v4 heart-rate sensor and Garmin's full health tracking.
items.flop: Most people don't know the Plus exists, and it gets priced like the base Venu 2. The speaker and mic are the bits that make it feel like a proper smartwatch.
items.catch: Battery replacement through Garmin costs about £100, so check battery health. Proprietary charger, no wireless charging, GPS lock can be slow.
items.why: The cheapest Garmin that feels like a smartwatch rather than a training tool.

items.name: Google Pixel Watch (1st gen)
items.spec: Lovely domed design, Wear OS with the Fitbit health stack, and it works well with Pixel phones.
items.flop: It was dismissed for weak battery life at launch, and now it has a better reason to be cheap: Google's guaranteed support ended in October 2025 with a final minor update, and it stays on Wear OS 5.1.
items.catch: Battery can come in under a day with always-on display, and age has made that worse. No more feature updates. Apps still update through the Play Store, but security fixes have stopped.
items.why: Listed as a warning. Earlier notes called this a sleeper. That stopped being true when support ended, so it is now a discount with a real reason behind it.

items.name: Samsung Galaxy Tab S8 Ultra
items.spec: 14.6in 120Hz AMOLED screen, Snapdragon 8 Gen 1, S Pen in the box, DeX desktop mode, quad speakers. Still one of the biggest, best tablet screens you can buy.
items.flop: Huge, expensive and Android at a time when buyers spending £1,000 went to iPad Pro. Most people never even picked one up.
items.catch: It has had its last major update (One UI 8 / Android 16), and security patches are due to stop around February–March 2027. Check the screen for burn-in and the corners for flex. The keyboard cover's touchpad is twitchy.
items.why: Great for showing clients tours and plans across the table. Buy it, use it for a season, then sell it before the end of security support hits resale.

items.name: OnePlus Pad
items.spec: 11.6in 144Hz screen in a 7:5 ratio, Dimensity 9000, quad speakers, a big battery and fast charging. Very quick for the price.
items.flop: OnePlus's first tablet, launched quietly into a market that buys iPads or Samsung. Plenty of reviewers liked it, but few buyers ever heard of it.
items.catch: The keyboard and stylus accessories can be unreliable. Check which Android version and security patch it is on before buying. Some connectivity features were missing at launch.
items.why: Good second screen for media and notes at about the price of a basic iPad.

items.name: Apple iPad Air 5 (M1, 2022)
items.spec: The same M1 that powers the Air and the mini, in a 10.9in tablet. Full Apple Pencil 2 support, USB-C, and enough power that it never feels like the limiting factor for anything a tablet is asked to do.
items.flop: Apple has pushed out an M2 Air, an M3 and now an M4, each one a modest step, and the Air line gets refreshed often enough that any given generation is old within eighteen months regardless of how capable it still is.
items.catch: 64GB base is tight if you are storing anything locally. Check it is removed from the previous owner's Apple ID or it is a brick. Inspect the corners, since a dropped iPad bends before it cracks and a bent chassis stresses the screen.
items.why: Flip. Strong, steady demand and an easy sell, because "M1, same chip as the MacBook" is a line any buyer understands. Also a decent on-site client viewer for walkthroughs.

items.name: Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio (1st gen)
items.spec: 14.4in 120Hz touchscreen on a pull-forward hinge (laptop, stage or flat canvas), pen support, and an RTX 3050 Ti in the i7 builds.
items.flop: The odd form factor confused reviewers, the performance was not class-leading for the money, and it only has two USB-C ports. The hinge is the selling point and nobody showed people how to use it.
items.catch: The i5 versions have no dedicated graphics, so check which one you are buying. Check the fabric hinge for wear and the pen for charging. Prices went up to £2,879 depending on spec, so compare like with like.
items.why: A drawing and presentation machine for design work at about the price of a mid-range laptop.

items.name: Lenovo ThinkPad T14s Gen 3
items.spec: 12th-gen i5 or i7 P-series, 14in 16:10 screen, Thunderbolt 4, the keyboard nothing else matches, and a chassis tested to military spec. Two generations back from the current A-List pick and still does the same job.
items.flop: Nothing went wrong with it. Lenovo shipped a Gen 4, then a Gen 5, and corporate fleets rotate on a three-year lease cycle, so thousands land on the market at once with the magazines already looking at the newer one.
items.catch: Ex-corporate means a BIOS supervisor password is possible and effectively unremovable, so confirm it boots to Windows setup. Soldered RAM on most configs, so buy the memory you need. Check the battery report before paying.
items.why: Business kit. The current editorial pick is the Gen 7 at £1,895. This is the same machine two revisions back for the price of a weekend's shooting.

items.name: Lenovo ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 10 / Gen 9
items.spec: Carbon fibre and magnesium at just over 1.1kg, 14in 16:10, Thunderbolt 4, and the best keyboard on any ultraportable. The flagship ThinkPad, which means the build quality the cheaper lines only approximate.
items.flop: Flagship depreciation is the steepest of any laptop class, because the buyers who pay £2,000 new are corporates who replace on schedule rather than on need. The X1 falls further and faster than the T-series sitting beneath it.
items.catch: Same BIOS password risk as any ex-corporate ThinkPad. Soldered RAM. The Gen 9 and Gen 10 look identical, so check the model year, since Gen 10 brought 12th-gen silicon and a better webcam.
items.why: Business kit, and the best laptop-per-pound on the list. The A-List's current X1 Carbon is £2,089. This is the same lineage at under a quarter.

items.name: Apple MacBook Air M1 (2020)
items.spec: The machine that started Apple silicon. Fanless, genuinely silent, 15 hours of real battery, and still quick enough for everything short of heavy video. Five years on it does not feel like an old laptop.
items.flop: Apple has shipped an M2, M3, M4 and M5 Air since, each one reviewed as the new best, and the M2 brought a redesign that made the M1 look dated. The chassis aged. The chip did not.
items.catch: 8GB is the common config and it is the real limit, not the chip. Check battery cycle count in System Information, and confirm it is signed out of iCloud and Find My or it is locked to the seller. Only two Thunderbolt ports and no HDMI.
items.why: Worth keeping. The cheapest route into a machine that still gets macOS updates, and the obvious second machine when your main one is tied up with a Pano2VR render.

items.name: Apple Mac mini M1 (2020)
items.spec: Same M1 as the Air with no battery or thermal limit, so it holds its clocks indefinitely. Gigabit ethernet, HDMI, two Thunderbolt ports, draws single-digit watts at idle and makes no noise at all.
items.flop: The M4 mini redesign got every headline and the M1 became the old square one. It also suffers from being a desktop nobody photographs, so it generates none of the resale enthusiasm a laptop does.
items.catch: Soldered RAM and storage, so 8GB and 256GB is what you get unless you pay up. Check it is signed out of the previous Apple ID. Some early units shipped with Bluetooth range issues that a firmware update largely fixed.
items.why: Business kit. The right shape for an always-on box: n8n, a local file server, or driving a screen, at a few watts and in total silence. The current A-List mini is £899.

items.name: Lenovo ThinkPad L14 / L15 Gen 3
items.spec: 12th-gen i5, a proper ThinkPad keyboard, and the thing the T-series gave up: user-serviceable RAM and storage on most configs. Tested against the same twelve military-grade requirements as the rest of the line.
items.flop: The L is Lenovo's budget ThinkPad, so it carries none of the X1 or T-series prestige and reviewers largely ignore it. It also sells in enormous corporate volume, which means it comes off lease in enormous volume.
items.catch: Ex-corporate, so check for a BIOS supervisor password. 8GB is the common config but unlike the T14s you can fix that for about £25. Heavier and thicker than a T-series, which is the trade for being able to open it.
items.why: Business kit, and the sensible first ThinkPad. Buy the cheapest 8GB one you can find, then pull RAM and an SSD from a dead EliteBook and it costs nothing to make right.

items.name: HP EliteBook 840 G8 / 845 G8
items.spec: 11th-gen i5 or i7, 14in, aluminium chassis, Wi-Fi 6, Bang and Olufsen audio and a genuinely good keyboard. The 845 is the Ryzen version and is usually cheaper for the same work.
items.flop: HP sells these to corporates by the tens of thousands and nobody buys one at retail, so there is no consumer enthusiasm to hold the price up. Three-year lease cycles then dump them all at once.
items.catch: Check for a BIOS password and for HP Sure Start lockouts on ex-fleet machines. The aluminium lid dents rather than cracks, so look for corner damage. Some configs have soldered RAM, so confirm before assuming you can upgrade.
items.why: Business kit. The cheapest route to a solid 14in work laptop, and the obvious donor if you want spare RAM and NVMe drives for the L14.

items.name: Dell OptiPlex Micro 7070 / HP EliteDesk 800 G5 Mini
items.spec: A litre of desktop with a 35W T-series i5, room for 32GB and an NVMe drive, and a proper internal power supply or an external brick. Silent, VESA-mountable behind a monitor, and they run for years.
items.flop: Corporate desktop fleets are replaced on schedule and these come out by the pallet. Nobody photographs a small black box, so they generate no resale enthusiasm and get listed as "office PC" with no model number at all.
items.catch: Confirm the power adapter is included, since these use proprietary bricks. 9th-gen Intel is the Windows 11 cutoff, so a 7060 or older will not be supported. Listings rarely state the exact generation, which is where the title badge earns its keep.
items.why: Business kit, and the Dell and HP answer to the ThinkCentre Tiny already on this list. Under £120 it is the cheapest always-on machine worth owning: n8n, a Plex box, or the brains behind a pub screen.

items.name: Asus Zenfone 10
items.spec: Flagship Snapdragon 8 Gen 2 in a 5.9in body, a gimbal-style stabilised main camera, a headphone jack, IP68 and wireless charging. Proper small phones barely exist any more.
items.flop: Small phones don't sell, and Asus barely marketed it in the UK. Reviewers mostly said it was too expensive, but that is not a problem at used prices.
items.catch: Charging is slow and still photos are average. No Android 16, so it stays on Android 15, though Asus was still sending security patches in September 2026. Check the patch date in settings.
items.why: For anyone who wants flagship speed in one hand. Nothing else this compact matches it at this price.

items.name: Sony Xperia 1 V / 5 V
items.spec: 4K OLED, a real continuous optical zoom, full manual camera controls with proper shutter and ISO dials, a headphone jack, and a microSD slot. Nothing current offers that combination.
items.flop: Sony barely advertises phones in the UK and sells them through almost no carriers. Without a contract deal in front of people, a £1,299 phone with no brand heat simply does not sell.
items.catch: The depreciation that makes it a bargain also makes it a terrible flip. Repair network in the UK is thin and parts are slow. Check the USB-C port for wear and the screen for green tint at low brightness.
items.why: Keep. Buy it to use for years, not to move on.

items.name: Ricoh Theta Z1
items.spec: Two 1-inch sensors, RAW DNG stills and adjustable aperture. Still the best image quality you can get from a pocket 360 camera, and it is still sold new for around £899.
items.flop: A niche product with almost no consumer marketing. It looks old next to Insta360's constant releases, so used prices have dropped while the new price has barely moved.
items.catch: Battery drains fast and is sealed in. Some units have been reported dying without warning, so test it properly before buying. Check whether it is the 19GB or 51GB model. Video is weak, so this is a stills camera.
items.why: Business kit for virtual tours: a pro-quality 360 image for less than half the new price, and faster than bracketing on a panoramic head.

items.name: Canon EOS RP
items.spec: 26MP full-frame sensor, Dual Pixel autofocus, a fully articulating screen and RF mount, so it takes adapted EF lenses without trouble. Light enough to carry everywhere.
items.flop: It was the 'cheap' full-frame camera and got judged against the R6 and Sony's A7 III. Spec-sheet reviews punished it for weak video, and good stills users never gave it a look.
items.catch: No in-body stabilisation. 4K is cropped 1.6x and loses Dual Pixel AF. Battery is rated at only about 250 shots, so buy spares. Burst shooting is slow.
items.why: The cheapest way into full frame and Canon RF. Very good for interiors on a tripod, where none of its weaknesses matter.

items.name: DJI Osmo Action 4
items.spec: 1/1.3in sensor, 10-bit D-Log M, strong low-light performance for an action camera, magnetic quick-release mounts and front and rear screens.
items.flop: GoPro dominates action cameras, and DJI replaced the Action 4 within a year. It now sits on DJI's discontinued list, which scares people off for no real reason.
items.catch: The DJI app needs activating before first use, and some Android phones have trouble connecting. Battery and heat reports are mixed. Check the lens cover for scratches.
items.why: Plenty of demand from cyclists and divers, so it sells within a fortnight if bought at the bottom of the range.

items.name: Shure MV7 (1st gen)
items.spec: Dynamic broadcast capsule that works over both USB and XLR, with Shure's auto-level and processing through the MOTIV app. It rejects the room well, which is the whole point in an untreated office.
items.flop: Shure replaced it with the MV7+, discontinued the original, and the used price fell straight through. It is the same capsule that made people pay £259 for it.
items.catch: No stand in the box. The touch panel is awkward and easy to brush by accident. Speak close and on-axis, because it isn't built for picking up a room. Check the micro-USB socket, which the MV7+ replaced with USB-C.
items.why: The best-sounding desk mic for calls, voiceovers and podcasts at this price, and the XLR output means it grows with you.

items.name: Elgato Wave:3
items.spec: Condenser capsule with Clipguard, which blends in a lower-gain backup signal so a sudden shout or laugh doesn't distort. Capacitive mute on top, and the Wave Link software gives you a proper virtual mixer for calls and recording.
items.flop: It was marketed as streamer kit, so office and voiceover users never looked at it. Gamers moved on, and used examples are plentiful and cheap.
items.catch: Some owners report dropouts, crackling and gain resetting, which are usually software issues, so update Wave Link first. As a condenser it picks up the room, so it needs a quiet space or close placement.
items.why: Plug-and-play desk mic with a built-in software mixer for well under half its launch price.

items.name: Rode NT-USB Mini
items.spec: Studio-quality condenser with a zero-latency headphone output, a magnetic desk stand and Rode Connect software that can run up to four of them at once on one computer.
items.flop: Small, plain and sold on almost no advertising beside louder RGB gaming mics, so it never built a following.
items.catch: No mute button. It picks up the room, so keep it close and turn the gain down. A few units have been reported failing, so test before paying.
items.why: The cheapest properly good desk mic. Buy two for two-person recording through Rode Connect.

items.name: HyperX QuadCast S
items.spec: Four polar patterns (cardioid, stereo, omni, figure-8), built-in shock mount, tap-to-mute and a gain dial on the base.
items.flop: It was bought on RGB hype, and gamers sell it on as soon as they upgrade. There are a lot of them on the used market, and buyers treat them like toys.
items.catch: Very sensitive to background noise, and the internal pop filter doesn't do much. The RGB software only runs on Windows. Some owners report USB connection drops after the warranty ends.
items.why: Constant demand from new streamers, so it moves quickly at the bottom of the range.

items.name: Audio-Technica AT2020USB+
items.spec: The classic AT2020 studio condenser with its own built-in converter, a headphone output and a mix dial. Needs no software and works on anything.
items.flop: It has been on sale so long it fell out of the conversation, and newer USB mics with RGB and apps took the reviews. The capsule is still excellent.
items.catch: No internal pop filter, so plosives come through, and you will want a foam windshield. It picks up keyboard clicks if it sits on the same desk, so put it on an arm. Check the cable and socket.
items.why: A no-fuss mic that just works on Mac, PC or iPad for voiceovers and calls.

items.name: Rode PodMic (XLR)
items.spec: End-address dynamic mic built like a tank, with an internal pop filter and a broadcast tone that ignores the room. It needs an interface, which pairs it naturally with the Scarlett 2i2 already on this list.
items.flop: XLR-only puts off people who want USB, so it got overlooked. The USB version that came later pushed the original further down the price list.
items.catch: Heavy, so it needs a sturdy arm. The swing mount sits close to the XLR socket, which makes some plugs awkward. Dynamic mics need gain, so a weak interface will sound thin.
items.why: Pair one with a used Scarlett 2i2 and you have a broadcast-sounding setup for under £120 all in.

items.name: Logitech Brio 4K webcam
items.spec: 4K sensor, HDR, Windows Hello face login and adjustable field of view. Still sharper than most new 1080p webcams.
items.flop: Logitech has released so many webcams since that the Brio looks old, and office clear-outs keep a steady supply on the market.
items.catch: The autofocus can lock onto the wall behind you if you sit off-centre, so set focus manually in Logi software. Check the detachable USB cable is included, since it is a slightly unusual type.
items.why: Client calls and tour walkthroughs that look like you made an effort, for the price of a cheap webcam.

items.name: Sony WH-1000XM4
items.spec: Class-leading noise cancelling for its time, multipoint pairing, 30-hour battery, speak-to-chat, and it folds, which the XM5 doesn't.
items.flop: The XM5 and then the XM6 pushed it down the list. Plenty of people still rate it above the XM5 for comfort and the folding case.
items.catch: Check the headband hinges and the ear pads, which wear. Battery will have aged. Some owners report failures, so buy from someone who will let you test it.
items.why: Lots of buyers know the name, so it moves quickly at under £100.

items.name: Sony WF-1000XM4 earbuds
items.spec: Strong noise cancelling, LDAC and a firmware update that added multipoint. It was the best buds of its year.
items.flop: The prices look like a bargain because many of these units have dying batteries. That is not under-marketing.
items.catch: Owners report batteries fading badly, charging problems, and one earbud cutting out after 15–20 minutes. The £20 listings are usually exactly that fault. You can't replace the batteries.
items.why: Listed as a warning. Spend the money on the over-ear WH-1000XM4 instead.

items.name: Kindle Oasis (3rd gen)
items.spec: 7in 300ppi screen with adjustable warm light, physical page-turn buttons, aluminium body and waterproofing. The only Kindle with proper buttons.
items.flop: Amazon discontinued it without a replacement and moved everyone to the Paperwhite and Scribe. People who know what it is want one, but there is no marketing pushing them.
items.catch: Micro-USB, not USB-C. Battery reports are mixed, so check idle drain. Check it is not still registered to the seller's Amazon account.
items.why: A typical drawer item: bought as a gift, used for one holiday, then shelved. Usually in good condition.

items.name: Samsung Galaxy Watch5 Pro
items.spec: Titanium case, sapphire glass, big 590mAh battery good for two to three days, GPX route import and turn-by-turn navigation. Pairs well with your Tab S9 and any Samsung phone.
items.flop: Samsung didn't make a Watch6 Pro, so the Pro line just vanished from shelves and people forgot about it. It is still the toughest Galaxy Watch made before the Ultra.
items.catch: Check which Wear OS version it is on and that it is not locked to the seller's Samsung account. Battery, GPS and connection reports vary. LTE versions cost a little more and need an eSIM sorted.
items.why: A premium titanium smartwatch for less than the price of a basic fitness band.

items.name: Canon EF-S 10-18mm f/4.5-5.6 IS STM
items.spec: Ultra-wide 16–29mm equivalent on APS-C, with image stabilisation, quiet STM focus and light weight. It adapts to Canon RF bodies too.
items.flop: A plastic, cheap-looking lens that everyone assumed was a compromise. It is actually sharp, and with DSLRs going out of fashion, used prices dropped.
items.catch: Plastic mount. Chromatic aberration, barrel distortion and dark corners at 10mm, all of which correct easily in Lightroom. Full-frame RF bodies will crop to APS-C.
items.why: The cheapest proper interiors lens there is, for estate agent and venue photography.

items.name: Wacom Intuos Pro Medium (PTH-660)
items.spec: Pro Pen 2 with 8,192 pressure levels and tilt, Bluetooth or wired, eight ExpressKeys, a touch ring and multi-touch. It is the same pen tech as Wacom's expensive Cintiqs.
items.flop: Pen displays took all the attention, and the plain tablet looked old-fashioned. Retouchers still swear by it.
items.catch: The textured surface wears out nibs quickly, so buy spares. Bluetooth can be flaky, so use the cable. Make sure the pen is included, because a replacement costs a lot.
items.why: Good for retouching tour panoramas and editing in Photoshop, and better for your wrist than a mouse.

items.name: Logitech MX Master 3
items.spec: MagSpeed electromagnetic scroll wheel, thumb wheel for horizontal scrolling, three-device switching and app-specific button profiles. It works on glass.
items.flop: The 3S and 4 replaced it with quieter clicks, and offices sell off the old ones in batches.
items.catch: Some report scroll wheel accuracy and Flow reliability issues. Check rubber grip wear and battery health. USB-C charging, so no adapter hassle.
items.why: Cheap upgrade for anyone still on a basic mouse. You will notice it in Photoshop and spreadsheets.

items.name: Garmin Venu 2 / 2S
items.spec: AMOLED screen, Elevate v4 heart-rate sensor and the full Garmin health suite. With a fresh battery it is a current-feeling smartwatch again.
items.flop: Garmin's official battery service costs about £100, which wipes out the value for a normal owner. So tired units get sold cheaply or put in a drawer.
items.catch: Battery tabs are soldered to the board, so desolder carefully to avoid damaging the flex cable. After service it is splash-resistant only unless the seal is pressure-tested: daily wear, no swimming. Tell the buyer that.
items.why: The original recipe from the watch notes. It is the core of this section and where the method was proven.

fix.tools: Craft heat gun on low, plastic picks, soldering iron, 3M 9448A adhesive gasket, IPA for cleanup

items.name: Garmin Fenix 5 / 5 Plus
items.spec: Steel-and-glass Fenix build, full GPS and, on the 5 Plus, maps, music and Garmin Pay. It's still an excellent outdoor watch once the battery is fresh.
items.flop: Two generations newer and on its second battery-life complaint cycle. Owners assume it is finished and trade it in for pennies.
items.catch: The battery is glued in and needs careful prying. Some aftermarket cells run slightly oversized, so test-fit before closing. Owners report part 361-00097-00 at either 230 or 255mAh, so check the capacity listed. The screwed rear case reseals better than a glued screen, but it is still not a factory seal.
items.why: A screwed caseback makes this the easiest Garmin to service well. A good second project after the Venu.

fix.tools: T6 Torx driver, plastic opening pick, replacement rear gasket if available

items.name: Garmin Forerunner 945
items.spec: Flagship training stack, maps, music, Garmin Pay and a strong GPS. Runners still rate it highly, and the 955 never felt like a big enough step up.
items.flop: Battery fade after five-plus years of heavy training use, with no cheap official fix. That is all that's wrong with most of them.
items.catch: Opening it compromises water resistance, and that matters for triathletes who swim. Battery listings are mostly 'compatible' cells, so buy from a seller with returns.
items.why: The best margin of the Garmin swaps, because runners know the 945 name and pay for it.

fix.tools: Precision screwdriver set, plastic picks, gentle heat, adhesive

items.name: Garmin Vivoactive 4 / 4S
items.spec: Garmin Pay, music, GPS and a proper touchscreen. It's the mainstream Garmin a lot of non-runners bought.
items.flop: Sold to casual users who replace rather than repair. Faulty units show up on eBay for as little as about £14 as parts-only.
items.catch: The screen adhesive needs 5–10 minutes of heat. Watch the screen ribbon and small connectors. No soldering, according to iFixit, which makes it easier than the Venu 2.
items.why: Cheapest way in and the easiest Garmin to buy dead. Good volume item.

fix.tools: Heat gun and iOpener, thin opening tool, spudger, Phillips #00

items.name: Sony WH-1000XM3
items.spec: Noise cancelling that was the best on the market in its year, comfortable, and USB-C. Plenty of people still prefer its sound to the XM4's.
items.flop: The battery goes, owners assume the headphones are finished, and they buy XM5s. It's the classic dead-battery headphone.
items.catch: Discharge below 25% before opening. Put the new adhesive in the housing, not on the cell. Check the headband hinge for cracks, which a battery won't fix.
items.why: Quick, low-skill job with steady demand. Good one to do several of in a batch.

items.name: Bose QuietComfort 35 II
items.spec: Still one of the most comfortable noise-cancelling headphones ever made, with simple controls and a huge user base.
items.flop: Battery fade, flaking headband and peeling ear pads make it look worn out. Most of that is cheap to fix.
items.catch: iFixit rates it Difficult, with soldering and adhesive. Shield the speaker from heat. Budget for new pads and a headband cover, otherwise it won't resell at the top of the range.
items.why: Only worth it if you're quick with a soldering iron. If you're doing pads and headband anyway, add the battery.

fix.tools: Hairdryer or heat gun (keep it under 100°C), soldering iron, opening pick, spudger, Phillips #00

items.name: Dyson V10 / V11 cordless
items.spec: Strong suction, LCD runtime display on the V11, and a huge range of accessories still on sale.
items.flop: When the battery dies, people assume the vacuum is dead and replace the whole thing. That makes this the most common dead-battery listing on Facebook Marketplace.
items.catch: V11s come with either click-in or screw-in packs, so check for the big red release button before ordering. Use genuine Dyson packs (about £85–£110). Cheap aftermarket packs are a fire and reputation risk. Check the motor and filters too.
items.why: Highest volume in this section and the easiest job here. The margin depends on buying the dead ones cheaply.

fix.tools: None for click-in packs; screwdriver for screw-in

items.name: Kindle Paperwhite (10th gen)
items.spec: 300ppi screen, waterproof and Audible support. Most people still don't need anything newer.
items.flop: Battery drain makes owners think it needs replacing, and a new Paperwhite is always on offer.
items.catch: The battery is glued in. Opening it breaks the waterproofing, so sell as 'not waterproof'. The margin is thin, so only buy at the bottom of the range.
items.why: Low-stakes practice piece. Good for learning the method before trying watches.

fix.tools: Plastic pry tools, hairdryer or low heat

items.name: Nintendo Switch Lite
items.spec: The whole Switch library on a compact handheld, with constant demand from parents.
items.flop: Faded batteries and 'won't charge' listings get written off as broken. Many are just the battery, or a dirty charging port.
items.catch: Strong adhesive: use only a few drops of IPA, because excess seeps under the screen. Diagnose first, since charge-port and stick-drift faults are common and are different repairs. Check it isn't banned or account-locked.
items.why: Sells all year and peaks before Christmas. Batch-buy in October.

fix.tools: Y00 tri-point, JIS 00, picks, spudger, plastic card, IPA (a few drops only)

items.name: iRobot Roomba 980 / 900 series
items.spec: Camera navigation, app control, carpet boost and room mapping. It was iRobot's flagship and has the build quality to match.
items.flop: A dead battery makes it look like the whole robot has failed. Owners have moved to robot-mop combos, and iRobot's troubles have put buyers off the brand.
items.catch: Use a compatible pack (4376392 / 4462425 part numbers). After fitting, charge to 100%, leave on charge two more hours, run it flat, then recharge. Check brushes, bearings and that the app still pairs.
items.why: The easiest swap on the page. Four screws, the largest margin per item, and the buyer just sees a working robot.
